children.text: Lipa Cathedral, formally the Metropolitan Cathedral of St. Sebastian, is the seat of the Archdiocese of Lipa in Lipa City, Batangas. Begun as an Augustinian convent in 1605, it moved with the town after a volcanic eruption, was heavily damaged in World War II, and was rebuilt in 1957.

The formal name of Lipa Cathedral is the Metropolitan Cathedral of St. Sebastian. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Lipa in the Poblacion of Lipa City, Batangas, and Wikipedia gives its coordinates as about 13.94° north and 121.16° east. Lipa is a basin city about
78 km
south of Manila (about
86 km
by road) at an elevation of about
, with an average temperature of about
and a dry season from January to April. This cool climate is said to be why Lipa was chosen as the seat of the diocese in 1910.

The cathedral's history begins on April 30, 1605, when the Augustinians accepted the site as the Convento de San Sebastian de Comintang, with Gabriel Rodriguez as its first prior. After a Taal Volcano eruption in 1724 residents relocated, and when the 1754 eruption submerged the new settlement of Balete under Taal Lake, the people moved inland to the present site, Mataas na Lupa ("high ground"). The move is told as a story of the faith and perseverance of the people of Lipa. The present church was built between 1779 and 1790 under Ignacio Pallares and Manuel Galiana, Manuel Diez Gonzalez completed the transept in 1865, and Benito Baras finished the building in 1894. In terms of the town's own records, Lipa began at Tagbakin in 1605, became a regular municipality in 1702, was elevated to a city in 1887 under Spanish rule, and became a chartered city on August 31, 1947. It is also passed down that the people walked to the new site praying the rosary.

In the twentieth century the cathedral went through two major changes. When the Diocese of Lipa was created on April 10, 1910, the church became a cathedral, and in 1944 it was heavily damaged during the Japanese occupation. After the war it was rebuilt to a design by Alejandro Olalla and Vergara and completed on December 14, 1957, when two side aisles were added. The Archdiocese of Lipa was raised to its present status on June 20, 1972. What we see today is therefore a nineteenth-century Spanish-era framework with a postwar reconstruction added to it.

The architecture is described as Neo-Renaissance, with a Latin cross plan, a large dome, and a row of arches. The octagonal bell tower beside the facade was first built with five floors and raised to seven in the postwar rebuilding, and the altars consist of one high altar topped with an image of St. Sebastian and four smaller side altars. Some sources call the style Neo-Renaissance and others Romanesque. A marker of the National Historical Commission was installed here in 1939, and restoration work on the roughly 220-year-old church and convent has also been recorded. Lipa's prosperity came with coffee. Don Galo de los Reyes, then the town head (governadorcillo), introduced coffee growing, and as a result Lipa was at one time counted as the richest town in the country. In the town center around the cathedral you can see traces of that prosperity together with everyday life today.

blocks.title: High altar and the image of St. Sebastian

children.text: Above the high altar at the far end is an image of St. Sebastian, the city's patron saint, with four smaller altars at the sides. It is busiest during masses for the city's big feast day on January 20.

blocks.title: Great dome and Latin cross interior

children.text: A great dome rises over the Latin cross plan, and arches run around the nave. The side aisles added in the postwar rebuilding make the interior spacious. Walk slowly and take in the rhythm of the arches and windows. For the exact structure and the dates of individual parts, check exhibit information or archdiocesan materials.

The bell tower beside the facade is octagonal and is said to have grown from five floors to seven in the postwar rebuilding. From the plaza side you can capture the whole church and the tower together in a photo.

blocks.title: Historical marker and signs of restoration

children.text: A National Historical Commission marker installed in 1939 is said to stand at the cathedral. You can read layers of time, tangled up with war and reconstruction, throughout the building.

blocks.title: A town that moved away from the volcano

children.text: Lipa moved to its present site after the Taal Volcano eruptions of 1724 and 1754. The cathedral is at the heart of this migration story, so it is more meaningful when seen together with the city's history.
The Lipa City fiesta honors the city's patron saint, St. Sebastian, and is held every January 20. Market stalls and cathedral masses make it crowded, so check the schedule ahead if you plan to visit.
The Museo de Lipa opened in November 2007 and is described as displaying coffee tools, gowns, antiques, and more. Visiting it along with the cathedral tells you about the city's coffee history.

Lipa prospered in the nineteenth century on coffee growing and was called the coffee granary of the Philippines. A Lomi Festival honoring the city's noodle dish and a coffee festival in December have also been held. This food story makes a fine companion to a cathedral visit.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: Half a day at the cathedral and in town

children.text: Take a bus bound for Lipa from Manila. Check companies and schedules at the terminal.
Arrive at Lipa Cathedral and look first at the facade and bell tower from the plaza.
Step inside and look quietly around the high altar, side altars, and dome. Refrain from taking photos during services.
Have an early lunch of Lipa coffee or lomi nearby.
Visit a town attraction such as Museo de Lipa. Check its opening hours.
Check the return bus time and leave early.
This schedule is only one example. The cathedral is a place of worship, so avoid visiting during mass.
See the story of the city's history at Lipa Cathedral early in the morning.
Travel by vehicle toward Taal Heritage Town. Travel time depends on traffic.
Have lunch in Taal and walk past the old houses and church.
Head home before dark, or stay in Batangas City.
Spanish-era sites are scattered around Batangas, so a vehicle is more convenient if you want to combine two or more in a day.
Buses run from Manila to Lipa and arrive at the grand terminal beside SM City Lipa. Check companies, schedules, and fares at the terminal.
From the grand terminal, take a tricycle or jeepney to the cathedral. Confirm the fare before you ride.
Lipa is about
78 km
from Manila. Travel time varies greatly with traffic.
By car you can continue from SLEX to the STAR Tollway, and the Jose P. Laurel (Ayala) Highway also passes through Lipa.
Tours that combine Batangas's historical sites sometimes appear, and contents and prices vary by operator.
The area around the cathedral is downtown, so parking can be difficult. Check locally.
In Lipa, tricycles, jeepneys, and multicabs run. For short distances you can also explore on foot.

Lipa has a tropical monsoon climate, with a dry season from January to April and rain the rest of the year. Annual rainfall is described as about 2,088 mm. Thanks to the cool temperatures you can visit year-round, but the dry season is more comfortable for walking.

On the city's feast day, January 20, the city is at its liveliest with cathedral masses and market stalls. If you want to see the architecture in peace, it is better to avoid this day, and if you want the festival atmosphere, aim for it. A coffee festival has also been held on December 11–16. Event dates change every year, so check.

In addition, the Walistik Festival has been held in the second week of January, and food events such as the Lomi Festival have been held in the city. Schedules may change every year. The cathedral itself is open year-round, but access may be controlled on major event days, so it is safest to check announcements from the city hall or the archdiocese just before you visit. In the rainy season, a useful trick is to finish the cathedral and the town in the morning and complete your travel before the afternoon rain.

Lipa is a large city with plenty of lodging and restaurants. From hotels near the cathedral to places around SM City Lipa there is a range of choices, so check rates by date on a booking site. Rooms may fill early around January 20.

The stars of the food scene are coffee and lomi. Lipa was called the coffee granary of the Philippines for its nineteenth-century coffee growing, and it is still remembered as a city famous for coffee. Lomi is described as the city's signature noodle dish. Taste and prices differ by shop, so consult local advice.
After visiting the cathedral, it is also nice to rest at a nearby market or café and watch everyday life in the city.

Lipa is growing as an institutional, medical, and commercial center with hospitals, commerce, and service industries, so lodging and conveniences are easy to find. It is cooler than Manila, which makes daytime walks more pleasant. Rather than seeing only the cathedral and leaving, we recommend a loop through the town's museum, cafés, and market so you also see the city as it is today.
The cathedral is a place of worship, so modest clothing that covers the shoulders and knees is recommended.
During mass, refrain from loud noise and photography and follow instructions.
For photos of the exterior, include the bell tower along with the plaza.
Check opening hours and mass schedules on cathedral announcements.
The January 20 feast day is very crowded, so allow extra time.
In town, keep your valuables and phone safe.
The light in the morning or at dusk is better for photos than the hot midday sun.
The inside of the cathedral is generally quiet, so silence your phone and take calls outside.
The cathedral is still a place of worship where masses are held. Viewing and photography may be restricted during services, so respect the instructions.
Check opening hours and mass times locally.
Bus times and travel times vary with traffic, so check your return transport in advance.
In the rainy season, typhoons or heavy rain can delay travel.
Downtown, watch out for pickpockets and traffic congestion.
On feast days there may be traffic controls for safety and crowd management.
